definition: Inputs minimally perturbed to cause confident misclassification (the panda-to-gibbon pixel noise).
details: Inputs minimally perturbed to cause confident misclassification (the panda-to-gibbon pixel noise). The founding demonstration that neural networks' decision boundaries do not match human perception; the LLM analogues are adversarial suffixes and jailbreak strings.

explainer.lead: Adversarial examples are inputs with tiny, deliberate changes that make an AI system produce a confidently wrong answer. They matter because a model can appear accurate while relying on decision boundaries very different from human perception.

tiers.eli5: Imagine changing a few dots on a picture of a panda so slightly that you still see a panda, but a computer becomes sure it is a gibbon. That tricked picture is an adversarial example. It shows that computers can notice patterns and make decisions in ways people do not.
tiers.practitioner: Use adversarial examples to probe classifier robustness and LLM safety rather than relying only on ordinary test inputs. For images, introduce a minimal perturbation and check the output and confidence; for LLMs, test adversarial suffixes and jailbreak strings. A model passing one set of attacks is not necessarily robust to differently crafted inputs.
tiers.paperLevel: Given a classifier f and an input x, construct x' = x + delta, where delta is small under a chosen constraint, so that f(x') differs from the correct output and may be confidently wrong. The panda-to-gibbon case illustrates this with minimal pixel noise. Smallness depends on the chosen constraint, and LLM adversarial suffixes and jailbreak strings are analogues rather than identical pixel-level attacks.

explainer.example: Minimal pixel noise is added to a picture of a panda. A person still sees a panda, but the neural network confidently classifies the altered image as a gibbon.

usedIn.name: Image-classifier security testing
usedIn.detail: Small pixel perturbations test whether a classifier can be pushed into a confident misclassification.

usedIn.name: Neural-network robustness research
usedIn.detail: Adversarial inputs expose differences between model decision boundaries and human perception.

usedIn.name: LLM red-teaming
usedIn.detail: Adversarial suffixes and jailbreak strings provide language-model analogues for probing unsafe or unintended behavior.

explainer.intuition: A model does not necessarily see an input the way a person does. A change that looks negligible to us can cross the model's decision boundary and flip its answer without appearing suspicious.
howItWorks: Start with an input the model would normally classify correctly.
Add a small, carefully chosen perturbation rather than an obvious alteration.
Keep the changed input perceptually almost identical to the original.
Feed it to the model and observe a different, often highly confident prediction.
explainer.whyItMatters: Adversarial examples demonstrate that neural-network decision boundaries can diverge sharply from human perception. They provide a concrete way to test whether confident model outputs remain reliable under deliberately crafted inputs.
misconceptions: The alteration does not have to be large or visible to a person.
An adversarial example is deliberately crafted, not merely any input a model gets wrong.
High confidence in the wrong answer does not mean the model has recognized the input correctly.
